title: Awful tunes and 'Annie Doesn't Live Here Anymore'
summary: Fats raged at the poor songs handed to him; Autrey recalls an irregular 17-bar chorus on which the band had no arranger to rely on.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well this -- of course one of the incredible things, I think, about the Fats Waller recordings, all through that period, is that he had so many awful tunes in there, terrible.

That we did, and he threatened, he's hit the piano, I won't do it! I won't do it! So the manager would come out. Now, Tom. Now, Tom. Especially Kirkpeby. Now Tom. And Thomas, now after all, but -- now, I -- for me. I think you should, and they would go through this business, you know. And he would say well, maybe so, all right, but he was --
Now for instance, I remember one tune, 'Annie Don't Live Here No More.'

Oh, God! Now we had to record things like that. And the meantime, what made it so hard, Dorseys -- one band, I want to check the other, they had arrangers. He had a guy who could sit down and write. He'd get a ridiculous tune. If the arranger should put this down on paper, it's no trouble. You play what you see. Yeah, you don't have to beat your brains out trying to think of ideas, or something, to

sell it. You play what you see and forget about it. You play whats on the paper (laughs). That's all you're required to do. Now if there's any squawk, give the arranger hell. Don't give me hell. (Laughs.) You know.
But when you get these dog tunes, and you don't have an arranger, what happens?
You've got more freedom, haven't you?

You've got -- you've got more freedom, but I mean you can't think of what you're going to do with it. I mean, a genius, you've got to be a genius to think something, and bring it out, and make it something. You know. You know, you -- in the first place, the whole idea is gone, is no good. You want to know who thought it up, why, and for what? And they want to -- no wonder they want to pay you to do it, because you've got to make -- you know, do what they didn't do.
Why do you -- why did you particularly remember 'Annie Doesn't Live here Anymore?' Is that -- something about that?

Seventeen -- 17 or 24 bar chorus, I mean it was irregular, and was nothing to it, I mean, so -- see, you're going to have a -- you must -- should have a 32 bar chorus. I mean to work with, to be sensible, or may -- well, you can probably understand it, and make somebody else understand what you're trying to do, or what you have done,

are doing, you know. Because when you get down to a 17 bar chorus, oh, my God! You know. Dah dah, dah, dah, dah dah -- and then, now we're going back to so and so, you don't mean it. He says oh, what's happening?
Well when does the meter run out? Or when -- how they going to get back in there?
In other words, it's hard to keep your place. You lose where you are.
You don't, because -- and you couldn't dance it, you couldn't sing it, you couldn't -- you don't plan nothing, you know. You know.
